title: Why can a bigger menu earn less?
principle: Every extra item you sell adds hidden costs.

screens.text: Let me take you to April 2020, when India was in lockdown. Britannia, the biscuit maker, could still run its factories, but with far fewer workers. It made many kinds of biscuits. Should it make a little of each kind, or focus on fewer kinds? Have a guess.

screens.prompt: With far fewer workers, which biscuits do you think Britannia chose to make?

options.label: Small amounts of every kind of biscuit
More of the biscuits people bought most
More new biscuits, to attract buyers

screens.why: It focused on its best sellers. Britannia made about one in five of its brands, like Good Day and Marie, and these brought in about 80% of its money. Making fewer kinds needed fewer workers. It also meant fewer things to buy, store and make.

screens.title: The cost you don't see
screens.text: Think of a baker's fridge. Every new item needs its own ingredients, space and recipe, and some go bad if they don't sell. These are complexity costs: they grow with every item, but don't show in any price. Each separate item is a SKU. More items can mean more cost.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: Now think about your home bakery in July of its fifth year. Your menu has 18 items: six cake flavours, cupcakes, cookies, breads, the party pack and more. Your chocolate cake sells for ₹850, and you keep ₹450. You're so busy you turn away about 3 chocolate orders a month.

screens.prompt: You sell 3 pineapple cakes a month, keeping ₹450 on each. But ₹1,000 of its fruit and cream goes bad. What do you really earn?
screens.why: Exactly. 3 cakes × ₹450 = ₹1,350. Take away the ₹1,000 of fruit and cream you throw away, and you earn only ₹350 a month from pineapple cakes. The waste is a hidden cost that never showed in the cake's price.

wrong.a: You worked out 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350. But that's before the waste. Take away the ₹1,000 of fruit and cream that goes bad, and you earn only ₹350 a month.
wrong.b: You don't lose money. 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350, and after taking away ₹1,000 of waste, you still earn ₹350 a month.

screens.prompt: Pineapple earns ₹350 and takes 5 hours a month. Those hours could bake 3 chocolate cakes you turn away, at ₹450 each. Which earns more?
screens.why: Right. 3 chocolate cakes × ₹450 = ₹1,350, almost four times pineapple's ₹350. Your time is a hidden cost too. When you spend 5 hours on pineapple, you can't use those hours for chocolate cakes that customers already want.

wrong.a: Variety can bring people in. But here people are already asking for chocolate, and you turn them away. 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350 beats the pineapple cake's ₹350.
wrong.c: Let's check. 3 chocolate cakes × ₹450 = ₹1,350. The pineapple cake earns ₹350. That's ₹1,000 more for the same 5 hours.

screens.prompt: Each cake's ₹400 covers its ingredients and box. I'll show you six costs. For each one, tell me: included in the ₹400, or extra?

items.text: The flour, sugar and cocoa in one cake
Cream you throw away because it went bad
The box you pack each cake in
Time you spend learning a new recipe
The cream on top of each cake
Fridge space for stock for 18 items

screens.why: Exactly. Flour, the box and the cream on top are part of the ₹400 cost. But wasted cream, learning time and fridge space are hidden extra costs that grow when you add items. That's why a long menu can eat your profit without you noticing.

screens.prompt: Your 8 best sellers bring most of your money. Selling only those, you'd need ₹6,000 of stock, not ₹15,000. What would that cut give you?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹15,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹9,000 you no longer need to keep in stock. As you use up the extra stock and don't buy it again, that cash comes back. Remember frozen cash from Unit 1: money in stock can't pay your bills. You get it back once, not every month.

wrong.b: Not every month. You get it back once. ₹15,000 minus ₹6,000 is ₹9,000 of cash that no longer sits on a shelf, the frozen cash from Unit 1.
wrong.c: Stock is money you've already spent. ₹15,000 minus ₹6,000 means ₹9,000 you no longer have to keep tied up on a shelf. That's cash you can use.

screens.setup: It's July, and you're fully booked, so any new work must replace something you bake now. Four customers ask for mango cake. You could sell about 6 a month, baking them together in 5 hours, and earn ₹2,100 after wasted mango. Pineapple earns ₹350 and coffee cake ₹150, each using 5 hours. Any 5 free hours could bake the 3 chocolate cakes you now turn away: ₹1,350.
screens.question: What do you do about the mango cake?

options.label: Add mango, keep every cake
options.outcome: Mango earns ₹2,100. But you need 5 hours to bake it, so you make 3 fewer chocolate cakes and lose ₹1,350 from those orders. You gain ₹750 a month, and your menu grows to 19 items.
options.why: Mango was a good add. But every new item brings new hidden costs, here 5 hours of your time, so it should push out a weak item.
options.better: Add mango, and drop pineapple and coffee.

options.label: Add mango, drop pineapple
options.outcome: You lose pineapple's ₹350, but mango earns ₹2,100. Mango takes the 5 hours you used for pineapple, so you can't bake extra chocolate cakes. You gain ₹1,750 a month. Coffee still earns only ₹150 for 5 hours, and your menu stays at 18 items.
options.why: A good swap, but you kept one weak item. Coffee's 5 hours could have baked 3 chocolate cakes, ₹1,350, instead of ₹150.
options.better: Add mango, and drop pineapple and coffee.

options.label: Add mango, drop pineapple and coffee
options.outcome: You give up the ₹500 from pineapple and coffee, and mango earns ₹2,100. Dropping both frees 10 hours. Mango takes 5, and in the other 5 you bake the 3 chocolate cakes you used to turn away: ₹1,350. You gain ₹2,950 a month, and your menu drops to 17 items.
options.why: Exactly. You let a new item in only by pushing out two weak ones. Your menu got shorter, your waste fell, and your hours went to cakes people want.

screens.text: Your menu grows from 18 items to 25. Sales may rise, but your ___ grows too. You have more waste, more stock and more ___.
screens.why: Exactly. That's complexity cost. Before you add an item, ask what it will really cost in waste, stock and hours, and what you could drop to make room.

summary: Complexity cost: every extra item (SKU) adds waste, stock and time that its price doesn't show.
Count what an item really earns: profit on each sale, minus the waste and the hours it takes.
Let a new item in only by pushing out a weak one.

cards.front: A cake earns you ₹900 a month, but ₹700 of its stock goes bad. What does it really earn?
cards.back: ₹900 minus ₹700 of waste is ₹200. Waste is a hidden cost.

cards.front: Customers ask for a new flavour. What's the smart way to add it?
options: Add it, and drop a slow item
cards.back: Every extra item adds hidden costs. Let a new one in by pushing a weak one out.

options: Each separate item you stock and sell
cards.back: SKU means stock keeping unit: each separate item you sell. More SKUs, more hidden cost.

sources.label: With limited workforce, Britannia working on 65% of its capacity (Agro & Food Processing, April 2020)
Britannia's focus on production of 20% brands amid lockdown brought in 80% revenue (DNA, 2021)
